Hi, Juan.  I'm ccing the Stan users and Stan developers lists because these are important general questions.  Here are my answers:

1.  For examples of multilevel modeling (which can be viewed as Bayesian) see my book with Hill.
For many more examples of Bayes, see by book with Carlin et al.
For management in particular, you could see this forthcoming article:  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/bayes_management.pdf

2.  There's Bayesian Data Analysis and the Stan manual.  Beyond that, no tutorial materials.  Bob and I are talking about writing a Statistics Using Stan book but this hasn't happened yet.  We do have plans for Stan short courses, though.  We will charge money for these; they are a way for us to raise funds to support the Stan project.  

A

On Feb 5, 2014, at 7:05 PM, Juan Fajardo wrote:

Dear professor Gelman,
I'm a Ph.D. student in management and visit your blog once a week as I'm trying to learn about bayesian analysis. I would very much appreciate if you could help me with answers to these two questions
1. How relevant is bayesian analysis in management. I mainly use regression and ANOVA with a frequentist approach, but I do not see a clear inflexion point where researchers start using bayesian versions of theses analysis regularly. Even though we can read call for this in journals like Management Science and call for papers like this (http://www.sagepub.com/upm-data/50351_JOM_SICall_Bayesian_ZyphurOswald9_11_12.pdf) in the journal of Management.
2. Is there a course to learn RStan? Or a video en youtube with an introduction to RStan? Or a resource such as "Learning RStan for dummies?" :)
Thank you very much.
Best
Juan

On 2/5/14, 10:03 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, Juan. I'm ccing the Stan users and Stan developers lists because these are important general questions. Here are
> my answers:
>
> 1. For examples of multilevel modeling (which can be viewed as Bayesian) see my book with Hill.

I would second the recommendation for Andrew and Jennifer's regression book.
It's what got me over the hump of understanding the models. After that,
Bayesian Data Analysis is a good step. I like Peter Hoff's intro to Bayesian
stats better than all the other introductory books specifically aimed at
Bayes.

> For many more examples of Bayes, see by book with Carlin et al.
> For management in particular, you could see this forthcoming article:
> http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/bayes_management.pdf

There's also the BUGS book. And the Congdon books have a gazillion
examples, but they're very terse on modeling decisions --- it's more
just how to implement them all in BUGS.
> 2. There's Bayesian Data Analysis and the Stan manual. Beyond that, no tutorial materials. Bob and I

> are talking
> about writing a Statistics Using Stan book but this hasn't happened yet.

> We do have plans for Stan short courses,
> though. We will charge money for these; they are a way for us to raise funds to support the Stan project.

Yes, but we'll give away the teaching materials for free, right?

The manual provides an introduction to Stan and its use, but it
assumes you already know the modeling fairly well --- it's more
about how to implement models in Stan than about the models themselves.

- Bob
